body.heading: A pattern machine
paragraphs: Point a kaleidoscope at the light, turn it slowly, and perfect symmetrical patterns bloom and melt and bloom again — never the same twice, never messy once. There is no drawing skill inside the tube and no computer. There are only mirrors, doing mathematics with light.

body.heading: Meet the parts
paragraphs: The mirror tunnel — three strips of mirror card taped into a triangle tube, shiny sides facing IN. This is the pattern engine. The object cup — a clear pot at the far end holding colourful beads, sequins and translucent bits that can tumble. The eye hole — a card disc with a small hole at the near end, so you look along the tunnel. The tube — the cardboard body that keeps the tunnel dark and straight.

body.heading: You will need
paragraphs: Three strips of mirror card the same size (a grown-up cuts and tapes them), a cardboard tube, a small clear plastic pot or two clear discs, colourful translucent beads and sequins, tape, and card for the eye disc.

paragraphs: Step 1 — A grown-up builds the tunnel: three mirror strips taped edge to edge into a long triangle, shiny sides in. Slide it into the cardboard tube — snug and straight.
Step 2 — Fit the eye disc. Tape a card disc with a small centre hole over one end of the tube. Look through it now: you can see the tunnel's triangle of mirrors waiting.
Step 3 — Load the object cup. Put a pinch of beads and sequins in the clear pot (not too many — they need room to tumble) and tape it over the far end so light shines through it.

Step 4 — Turn and watch. Point the far end toward the light — never the sun — and turn the tube slowly. The beads tumble, and the mirrors multiply them into a perfect six-petalled flower of colour that changes with every turn.

body.heading: The science bit
paragraphs: One mirror makes one reflection. But mirrors facing each other reflect each other's reflections — copies of copies, bouncing on and on. Three mirrors in a triangle bounce the beads' image around the triangle again and again, tiling it into a pattern with perfect symmetry: every petal matches because every petal IS the same beads, reflected. The pattern can never be messy — mirrors cannot reflect untidily — and it can never repeat exactly, because the beads never fall the same way twice.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Why are the patterns always symmetrical, even though the beads fall messily?
2. How many petals does your pattern have? What do you think decides that number — the beads, or the mirrors?

takeaway: Three mirrors in a triangle reflect each other's reflections, tiling a few tumbling beads into endless perfectly symmetrical patterns.
materials: Three strips of mirror card (grown-up cuts and tapes)
Small clear pot or two clear discs
supervision: A grown-up builds the mirror tunnel and supervises the whole project.
safetyNotes: Mirror CARD or acrylic only — never glass or real mirror shards in a child's kaleidoscope; cut edges of mirror card are taped over by a grown-up before the tunnel is handled.
Never point a kaleidoscope at the sun or look at the sun through it — it gathers light toward your eye. Bright windows and lamps are the light sources.
Beads and sequins are small parts — counted out and back into a closed pot, away from children under 3 and off the floor.
screenFreeExtension: Pattern copying game: one person turns the kaleidoscope to a favourite pattern and describes it — colours, petals, shapes — while the other draws what they hear. Then compare drawing to pattern.
